entries.meaning: Paraśurāma accuses Rāma of feigning humility while approving his brother’s harsh words, and demands satisfaction in battle. Rāma bows and smiles inwardly while the sage brandishes his axe. He accepts responsibility for Lakṣmaṇa’s offence, asks the sage to give up anger, and offers his own head to the axe: a master cannot properly fight his servant, and the boy spoke only after seeing the warrior’s dress.

Rāma explains that the sight of bow, arrows and axe made the boy answer in anger, mistaking Paraśurāma for a warrior; had he appeared as a sage, the child would have placed the dust of his feet upon his head. He asks forgiveness for an ignorant mistake and contrasts his own small name—Rāma, with only a bowstring—with Paraśurāma’s great, sacred name and nine Brahmin virtues. Paraśurāma retorts that Rāma too seems as contrary as his brother.

Paraśurāma says Rāma takes him for an ordinary Brahmin, then describes his warfare as a sacrificial rite: his bow is the ladle, arrows the oblations, wrath the fire, armies the fuel, and mighty kings the victims cut down with his axe. He rebukes Rāma’s pride after breaking the bow. Rāma replies that the old Pināka broke at a touch and gives him no cause for pride; if the charge is that they scorn Brahmins, no warrior in the world can make the Raghus bow from fear.

Rāma declares that if any god, demon, king or champion challenges him in battle, he will fight gladly, even if the opponent is Death; a Kṣatriya who shrinks from combat disgraces his lineage. Yet the Raghus fearlessly bow before the Brahmin line. These gentle but profound words lift the veil from Paraśurāma’s understanding. He offers Rāma Viṣṇu’s bow and asks him to draw it; the bow passes to Rāma of itself, dispelling doubt and revealing his divine power.

Thrilled and overflowing with love, Paraśurāma hails Rāma as the sun of Raghu’s lotus-line, the fire that burns demonic clans, protector of gods, Brahmins and cows, destroyer of pride, delusion, anger and error, and ocean of courtesy, virtue and compassion. He begs both brothers to forgive his ignorant words, praises Rāma repeatedly, and leaves for the forest to practise austerity. The frightened crooked kings slip away, while gods sound drums, shower flowers, and the people rejoice as the pain of delusion disappears.

Instruments resound and groups of lovely women sing like cuckoos. Janaka’s joy is beyond telling, as though a lifelong pauper had found treasure; Sītā becomes happy and fearless, like a young cakora at moonrise. Janaka bows to Viśvāmitra, credits his grace for Rāma’s breaking of the bow, and asks what should follow. The sage says the marriage already came into being when the bow broke, but Janaka should now observe family custom: consult Brahmins, elders and gurus, and invite Daśaratha.

At Viśvāmitra’s direction Janaka sends messengers to Ayodhyā to summon Daśaratha. He calls the leading citizens and orders every market, road, shrine and quarter of the city adorned, then commissions attendants and skilled artisans to erect wondrous canopies. Invoking the Creator, they begin with golden plantain pillars, emerald leaves and ruby flowers—work so marvellous that it seems to bewilder Brahmā himself.

The artisans fashion green jewelled bamboo so naturally jointed that it cannot be distinguished from living cane, and golden betel vines with beautiful leaves. Pearl strings hang among elaborate bonds; rubies, emeralds, diamonds and turquoise are cut and set into lotuses. Multicoloured bees and birds seem to hum and call as the wind moves. Carved divine figures stand upon the pillars bearing auspicious objects, while gem-made elephants fill the courtyards and sapphire foliage, golden blossoms and emerald clusters gleam upon silken cords.

entries.meaning: Fine festoons look like snares lovingly arranged by Love himself; auspicious jars, flags, banners, fabrics, fly-whisks and jewelled lamps beautify the pavilion. No poet can describe the hall where Vaidehī will be the bride and Rāma, ocean of beauty and virtue, the groom. Every house in Janaka’s city rivals the palace, and the splendour makes even the wealth of the gods seem small. Fortune herself appears to dwell there disguised as a noble woman; Sarasvatī and Śeṣa hesitate to describe the city.

Janaka’s messengers reach sacred Ayodhyā and are delighted by the lovely city. At the gate they deliver the letter; Daśaratha rises to receive it, reads with tear-filled eyes and a thrilled body, presses the fine letter bearing news of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to his heart, and for a time cannot speak. After he reads its true report aloud, Bharata and Śatrughna arrive and shyly ask where the message came from and whether their life-dear brothers are safe. Hearing their loving question, the king reads it again.
